examName: Developing AI Cloud Solutions on Azure
tagline: Build AI-enabled cloud apps on Azure: containers, vector data stores, messaging, and observability.

domains.name: Develop containerized solutions on Azure
domains.description: Build, store, and manage container images in Azure Container Registry; deploy containers to App Service, Azure Container Apps (with KEDA scaling), and Azure Kubernetes Service; and monitor and troubleshoot containerized workloads.

domains.name: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
domains.description: Use Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL with pgvector, and Azure Managed Redis to store and query data and embeddings, run vector similarity search, and implement retrieval for RAG.

domains.name: Connect to and consume Azure services
domains.description: Integrate Azure Service Bus and Event Grid for messaging and event-driven workflows, and build serverless APIs with Azure Functions triggers and bindings.

domains.name: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions

questions.stem: You have a Dockerfile for a Python inference API and an Azure Container Registry named contosoacr. You want to build the image and push it to the registry in the cloud, without installing or running a local Docker Engine. Which Azure CLI command should you run?

options.text: docker build -t contosoacr.azurecr.io/inference:v1 . && docker push contosoacr.azurecr.io/inference:v1
az acr build --registry contosoacr --image inference:v1 .
az acr task create --registry contosoacr --image inference:v1 --file Dockerfile .
az acr import --name contosoacr --source inference:v1

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A quick task with az acr build offloads the docker build to ACR in the cloud and pushes the image by default, so no local Docker Engine is required. Why the others are wrong: **A** runs docker locally, which needs a Docker Engine; **C** az acr task create defines a triggered task rather than running an on-demand build now; **D** az acr import copies an existing image from another registry, it does not build from a Dockerfile.

questions.stem: You defined a multi-step workflow in a file named acr-task.yaml that builds a Python image, runs a container of it to execute tests, and then pushes the image. The YAML is in a GitHub repo. Which Azure CLI command runs this multi-step task in Azure Container Registry?

options.text: az acr build --registry contosoacr -f acr-task.yaml https://github.com/contoso/app.git
az acr task run --name acr-task.yaml --registry contosoacr
az acr run --registry contosoacr -f acr-task.yaml https://github.com/contoso/app.git
az acr pack build --registry contosoacr --pull acr-task.yaml

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Multi-step tasks are defined in a YAML file and executed with az acr run, using -f to specify the YAML and a context such as a Git repo. Why the others are wrong: **A** az acr build builds a single image from a Dockerfile, not a multi-step YAML; **B** az acr task run executes a previously created named task, not a YAML file passed inline; **D** az acr pack build uses Cloud Native Buildpacks to build from source without a Dockerfile, not a multi-step YAML.

questions.stem: Your team commits Python code to a GitHub repository. You want Azure Container Registry to automatically rebuild the container image every time a commit is pushed to the main branch. Which approach configures this?

options.text: Run az acr build each time and rely on it to poll the repository for new commits.
Enable WEBSITES_PORT on the registry so it listens for GitHub push events.
Use az acr import with the repo URL to mirror commits into the registry.
Create a task with az acr task create, specifying the GitHub repo URL and a personal access token so ACR can register a webhook.

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A commit trigger is configured with az acr task create by supplying the Git context and a personal access token; ACR creates a webhook that fires a build on each commit. Why the others are wrong: **A** az acr build is a one-time on-demand build and does not watch the repo; **B** WEBSITES_PORT is an App Service container setting and is unrelated to registries or triggers; **C** az acr import copies images between registries, it cannot watch a Git repo.

questions.stem: Your Python container is built on the python:3.12-slim base image. You want Azure Container Registry to automatically rebuild and re-push your application image whenever that base image is updated, so OS and framework patches flow into your image. Which ACR Tasks capability provides this?

options.text: A timer trigger that rebuilds the image on a fixed schedule regardless of base image changes.
A base image update trigger, which detects updates to the parent image and rebuilds dependent images automatically.
A pull request trigger on the application's Git repository.
The az acr import command run manually after each base image release.

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** ACR Tasks tracks the base (parent) image dependency and, when the base image is updated, automatically rebuilds the application images that depend on it. Why the others are wrong: **A** a timer trigger fires on a schedule and is blind to base image updates; **C** a pull request trigger responds to PRs on source code, not to base image changes; **D** az acr import is manual and copies images, it does not detect base image updates.

questions.stem: You need to copy an existing image, mcr.microsoft.com/azure-cognitive-services/textanalytics/language:latest, into your private registry contosoacr so your deployments pull from a registry you control. You do not have a local Docker daemon available. Which command copies the image directly between registries?

options.text: docker pull mcr.microsoft.com/azure-cognitive-services/textanalytics/language:latest then docker push contosoacr.azurecr.io/language:latest
az acr build --registry contosoacr --image language:latest mcr.microsoft.com/...
az acr import --name contosoacr --source mcr.microsoft.com/azure-cognitive-services/textanalytics/language:latest --image language:latest
az acr run --registry contosoacr -f language:latest

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** az acr import copies an image from another registry (including MCR or Docker Hub) directly into your registry without a local docker pull/push. Why the others are wrong: **A** requires a local Docker daemon, which is unavailable; **B** az acr build builds from a Dockerfile context, not an existing remote image reference; **D** az acr run executes a multi-step YAML task and -f expects a YAML file, not an image tag.

questions.stem: In a CI pipeline you want ACR Tasks to validate that your Python image builds successfully on every commit, but you do NOT want the resulting image pushed to the registry during these validation runs. Which az acr build option achieves this?

options.text: Add the --platform Linux/amd64 flag to az acr build.
Omit the --image flag from az acr build.
Add --registry-only to az acr build.
Add the --no-push flag to az acr build.

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** az acr build pushes the built image by default; passing --no-push performs the build to validate it without pushing the result to the registry. Why the others are wrong: **A** --platform sets the target OS/architecture and does not affect pushing; **B** omitting --image affects tagging, not the push behavior, and a build still occurs; **C** --registry-only is not a valid az acr build flag.

questions.stem: You deploy a custom Linux container to Azure App Service. Your Python app uses Gunicorn and listens on port 8000 inside the container, but the site returns connection errors. By default App Service assumes the container listens on a different port. Which app setting do you configure so App Service routes HTTP requests to the correct port?

options.text: PORT_OVERRIDE = 8000
WEBSITES_PORT = 8000
WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE = 8000
DOCKER_CUSTOM_PORT = 8000

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** App Service assumes a custom container listens on port 80 by default; set WEBSITES_PORT to the port your container actually listens on, here 8000. Why the others are wrong: **A** PORT_OVERRIDE is not a recognized App Service setting; **C** WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE toggles persistent /home storage, not the port; **D** DOCKER_CUSTOM_PORT is not a valid App Service app setting.

questions.stem: Your Python container running on Azure App Service reads a connection string from an environment variable named AI_ENDPOINT at runtime. Without rebuilding the image, how do you supply this value so it is available to the container as an environment variable?

options.text: You must hard-code AI_ENDPOINT in the Dockerfile with ENV and rebuild, because App Service cannot pass environment variables to custom containers.
Store AI_ENDPOINT only in the App Service deployment slot name; it becomes an environment variable automatically.
Add an app setting named AI_ENDPOINT; App Service injects app settings into the container as environment variables at runtime.
Place AI_ENDPOINT in a file named .env in /home; App Service auto-loads it before any other configuration.
Set AI_ENDPOINT as a tag on the container registry repository.

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** App settings configured on the web app are automatically injected into the running container process as environment variables, so no image rebuild is needed. Why the others are wrong: **A** is false, App Service does pass app settings to custom containers; **B** a slot name is not an environment variable mechanism; **D** App Service does not auto-load a .env file from /home; **E** registry tags are image metadata and are never exposed as container environment variables.

questions.stem: Your Python web app on Azure App Service stores an API key in app setting AI_KEY. Security requires the secret live in Azure Key Vault while the app continues to read it from the AI_KEY environment variable with no code change. You set AI_KEY to @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://kv-contoso.vault.azure.net/secrets/ai-key). What else must be configured for the reference to resolve?

options.text: Store the vault's master key in the WEBSITES_PORT app setting.
Assign the app the Owner role on the entire subscription.
Disable managed identity so App Service uses the deployment credentials to read the vault.
Enable a managed identity on the app and grant it the Key Vault Secrets User role (or Get secrets permission) on the vault.

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A Key Vault reference resolves via the app's managed identity (system-assigned by default), which must be granted the Key Vault Secrets User RBAC role or the Get secrets access-policy permission. Why the others are wrong: **A** WEBSITES_PORT controls the container port, not vault access; **B** Owner on the subscription is excessive and is not the documented requirement; **C** the reference needs an identity with vault access, so disabling managed identity prevents resolution.

questions.stem: You want an Azure App Service app setting that references a secret named db-password in the Key Vault kv-contoso, always using the latest secret version. Which value uses the correct Key Vault reference syntax?

options.text: @KeyVault(kv-contoso/db-password)
@Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=kv-contoso;SecretName=db-password)
${KeyVault:kv-contoso:db-password}
@Microsoft.KeyVault(https://kv-contoso.vault.azure.net/db-password)

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A valid reference is @Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=<name>;SecretName=<name>); omitting the version makes App Service track the latest version. Why the others are wrong: **A** @KeyVault(...) is not the supported syntax; **C** uses a configuration-provider style that App Service does not recognize as a Key Vault reference; **D** the SecretUri form needs the SecretUri= prefix and the /secrets/ path segment, which this URL lacks.

questions.stem: You want Azure App Service to pull your container image from the private registry contosoacr using the web app's managed identity instead of storing a registry username and password. After enabling the identity and granting it the AcrPull role on the registry, which additional configuration tells App Service to use managed identity for the image pull?

options.text: Set the app setting DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_PASSWORD to the identity's client ID.
Set WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE to true.
Set the site property acrUseManagedIdentityCreds to true.
Add the AcrPush role to the identity in addition to AcrPull.

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** After granting AcrPull to the identity, you configure the site setting acrUseManagedIdentityCreds=true so App Service authenticates the image pull with managed identity. Why the others are wrong: **A** putting a client ID in a password setting still uses credential-based auth and is incorrect; **B** that setting controls persistent storage, not registry authentication; **D** AcrPush grants write access and is unnecessary for pulling an image.

questions.stem: You maintain several versioned tags of a Python image in Azure Container Registry, such as scoring:v1, scoring:v2, and scoring:latest. You need to remove only the scoring:v1 tag and its manifest from the repository to reclaim space. Which command should you use?

options.text: az acr build --registry contosoacr --image scoring:v1 --no-push .
az acr import --name contosoacr --source scoring:v1 --delete
az webapp config container delete --image scoring:v1
az acr repository delete --name contosoacr --image scoring:v1

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** az acr repository delete with --image <repo>:<tag> removes that tagged image (and its manifest) from the registry. Why the others are wrong: **A** az acr build creates an image, even with --no-push it does not delete anything; **B** az acr import copies images and has no --delete behavior for removing tags; **C** that command targets an App Service web app's container config, not registry contents.

questions.stem: You define a multi-step ACR task in YAML to build a Python image, run it for functional tests, and push it on success. Which task step types are valid in an ACR Tasks YAML file? (Select two.)

options.text: deploy
push
cmd
trigger

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, C):** ACR Tasks YAML supports the step types build (build images), push (push images), and cmd (run a container as a step, used for tests); push and cmd are both valid. Why the others are wrong: **A** deploy is not an ACR Tasks step type; deployment is handled outside the task or via a cmd step running a tool; **D** trigger is not a step type, triggers are configured on the task definition, not inside the steps list.

questions.stem: You are choosing how to externalize configuration for a Python container on Azure App Service. Which statements are correct about app settings and secrets for custom containers? (Select two.)

options.text: App settings can only be read by .NET apps and are never visible to a Python process.
App settings are injected into the running container as environment variables at runtime.
Setting WEBSITES_PORT is required for every app setting to be passed to the container.
An app setting value can be a Key Vault reference so the secret is stored in Azure Key Vault rather than in plain configuration.

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, D):** App Service injects app settings as environment variables into the container, and an app setting can be a @Microsoft.KeyVault(...) reference so the secret lives in Key Vault. Why the others are wrong: **A** is false, environment variables are language-agnostic and a Python process reads them normally; **C** WEBSITES_PORT only sets the container's HTTP port and is unrelated to whether app settings are passed.

questions.stem: You are taking a Python inference app from source to a running Azure App Service custom container that pulls from your own registry. Arrange the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Run az acr build to build the Python image and push it to Azure Container Registry.
Create the App Service web app and configure it to use the image from your registry.
Add an app setting (or Key Vault reference) supplying the runtime configuration the container expects.
Browse to the app's URL to confirm the container starts and serves requests.

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B, C, D):** Build and push the image first so it exists in the registry, then create the web app pointed at that image, then supply runtime configuration via app settings or Key Vault references, and finally verify by browsing. Why the others are wrong: **B** can't precede A with no image to pull; **C** configures an app that already references the image; **D** verification is only meaningful after the app and config exist.

questions.stem: Which technology does Azure Container Apps use under the hood to provide automatic, event-driven horizontal scaling against sources such as Azure Service Bus and Event Hubs?

options.text: The Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) configured directly
Azure Monitor autoscale rules on the App Service plan
Virtual Machine Scale Set autoscaling
KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling)

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Container Apps builds its declarative scaling on KEDA, which scales replicas based on HTTP/TCP load, CPU, memory, and event sources like Service Bus, Event Hubs, Kafka, and Redis. Why the others are wrong: **A** KEDA wraps the HPA, but you configure scale rules, not the HPA directly; **B** App Service autoscale is unrelated to Container Apps; **C** VMSS autoscaling scales VMs, not container replicas in this serverless platform.

questions.stem: You deploy a container app that has no ingress and no scaling rule defined. You want to guarantee that at least one replica is always running so a background worker keeps processing. What should you configure?

options.text: Set the maximum number of replicas to 1
Set the minimum number of replicas to 1 or higher
Set the HTTP concurrentRequests value to 0
Enable external ingress on the app

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The default minimum replica count is 0, so to keep an instance always running you set minReplicas to 1 or more. Without ingress and without a scale rule or minReplicas, the app scales to zero and cannot start back up. Why the others are wrong: **A** maxReplicas only caps the upper bound; **C** concurrentRequests sets the HTTP threshold, not a floor; **D** enabling ingress changes traffic exposure but does not force a minimum replica.

questions.stem: A container app uses a custom KEDA scale rule for an Azure Service Bus queue, with minReplicas set to 0. After the queue empties, replicas are not scaling back to zero as quickly as you expect. Which behavior setting governs how long Container Apps waits after the last event before scaling from the final replica to 0?

options.text: The polling interval (default 30 seconds)
The scale-up stabilization window (default 0 seconds)
The cool down period (default 300 seconds)
The concurrentRequests threshold

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The cool down period defaults to 300 seconds and is how long KEDA waits after the last event before scaling the app down to its minimum; it only takes effect when going from the final replica to 0. Why the others are wrong: **A** the polling interval controls how often event sources are queried, not the wait before scale-in; **B** the scale-up window affects scale-out decisions; **D** concurrentRequests applies to HTTP rules, not a Service Bus trigger.

questions.stem: You are authoring a custom KEDA scale rule for an Azure Storage queue trigger in a container app. Microsoft recommends a specific authentication approach to avoid storing connection strings in the app. Which approach should you use?

options.text: Embed the storage account key in the container image
Use managed identity for the scale rule
Pass the connection string as a plain environment variable
Disable authentication because queue scalers do not require it

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Container Apps scale rules for Azure resources like Queue Storage, Service Bus, and Event Hubs support managed identity, and Microsoft recommends it where possible so no secrets are stored in the app. Why the others are wrong: **A** baking keys into the image is insecure and unmanaged; **C** a plaintext connection string in an env var exposes the credential; **D** the scaler must authenticate to read queue length, so auth cannot be skipped.

questions.stem: Your container app is in multiple revision mode. You add a new scale trigger to the active revision and redeploy. What is the effect on revisions?

options.text: A new revision is created and the old revision remains available with its old scale rules
The existing revision is updated in place because scale rules are an application-scope change
No revision is created until you manually activate one
All inactive revisions are immediately purged

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Scale rules live in properties.template, so editing them is a revision-scope change that produces a new immutable revision; in multiple revision mode the old revision stays available with its prior rules. Why the others are wrong: **B** scale rules are revision-scope, not application-scope, and revisions are immutable; **C** the new revision is created on deploy; **D** inactive revisions persist up to the configured cap.

questions.stem: Which two changes to an Azure Container App are revision-scope changes that trigger creation of a new revision when you deploy? (Select two.)

options.text: Updating the container image to a new tag
Changing the value of an existing secret
Editing a scale rule on the app's template
Toggling ingress on or off

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Both the container image/configuration and scale rules are in properties.template, so changing them is a revision-scope change that creates a new revision. Why the others are wrong: **B** secret values live in properties.configuration, an application-scope change that applies to all revisions without creating one (existing revisions must be restarted to pick them up); **D** ingress configuration is also application-scope and does not create a new revision.

questions.stem: You want to gradually shift production traffic from the current revision of a container app to a new revision for a blue-green rollout, controlling the exact percentage each revision receives. What must you do first?

options.text: Set the app's active revisions mode to multiple
Keep the app in single revision mode and rely on automatic cutover
Delete the old revision before deploying the new one
Disable ingress so traffic can be split internally

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Traffic splitting requires multiple revision mode (set activeRevisionsMode to multiple), which keeps revisions active so you can allocate traffic percentages for blue-green rollouts. Why the others are wrong: **B** single mode does an automatic full cutover with no percentage control; **C** deleting the old revision removes your rollback target; **D** disabling ingress removes the HTTP endpoint traffic splitting distributes across.

questions.stem: You update the value of an existing secret on a container app that is running in single revision mode. The running container still reads the old secret value. What explains this and what is the correct remedy?

options.text: Secret values are revision-scope, so a new revision was created automatically and you just need to wait
A secret update is an application-scope change that does not create a new revision; you must restart the revision so the container picks up the new value
Secret changes require deleting and recreating the container app
Container Apps does not support changing secret values after creation

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Secret values are application-scope changes applied to all revisions without creating a new one, and a running revision must be restarted before its container recognizes the new value. Why the others are wrong: **A** secret values are application-scope, not revision-scope, so no new revision is created; **C** recreating the whole app is unnecessary; **D** secret values can be updated; they just require a revision restart to take effect.

questions.stem: You have a YAML manifest that declares a Deployment and a Service for an application you want to run on an existing Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster. Which command applies the manifest and creates the defined Kubernetes objects?

options.text: az aks create --file manifest.yaml
kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml
docker compose up manifest.yaml
az containerapp up --yaml manifest.yaml

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** kubectl apply -f parses the manifest and declaratively creates or updates the Kubernetes objects (Deployment, Service, etc.) on the cluster. Why the others are wrong: **A** az aks create provisions a cluster, not workloads from a manifest; **C** docker compose is for local Compose files, not Kubernetes objects on AKS; **D** az containerapp up targets Azure Container Apps, a different service, not AKS.

questions.stem: After applying a manifest to AKS, you run kubectl get service for your front-end Service and the EXTERNAL-IP column shows <pending> for a minute or two. Which manifest configuration causes Azure to provision a public IP for the Service?

options.text: The Service has type: ClusterIP
The Deployment sets replicas to a value greater than 1
The Service has type: LoadBalancer
The Pod template requests a hostPort

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A Service of type LoadBalancer triggers AKS to provision an Azure load balancer and assign a public EXTERNAL-IP, which briefly shows <pending> while it is created. Why the others are wrong: **A** ClusterIP exposes the Service only inside the cluster with no external IP; **B** replica count controls Pod scaling, not external exposure; **D** hostPort binds to a node port directly and does not provision a load-balanced public IP.

questions.stem: A pod on your AKS cluster is stuck in ImagePullBackOff. Which command gives you the most direct insight into why the kubelet cannot pull the image, by showing the pod's recent events and status?

options.text: kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl scale deployment <name> --replicas=0
kubectl rollout restart deployment <name>
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** kubectl describe pod shows the pod's status and its recent Events, where the kubelet records the image-pull failure reason (for example, authentication or a wrong image reference) so you can diagnose ImagePullBackOff. Why the others are wrong: **A** listing nodes shows node info, not the pod's pull error; **B** scaling to zero just stops the pods without explaining the failure; **C** restarting the rollout re-attempts the pull but does not surface the cause.

questions.stem: Your team needs to investigate an AKS incident that happened three hours ago by reviewing Kubernetes events from that time. They find kubectl get events returns nothing relevant. What is the underlying limitation, and how should you retain events for longer going forward?

options.text: Events are stored indefinitely; the cluster must be misconfigured, so recreate it
Kubernetes events are only available for about one hour and have no retention; enable Container insights (Azure Monitor) to store them longer
Events are retained for 30 days by default; the issue is an RBAC permission, not retention
Events persist on each node's disk; SSH into the node to read older events

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Kubernetes events have no built-in retention and are only available for about one hour after they are generated, so older events are gone; enable Container insights (Azure Monitor) to store them longer. Why the others are wrong: **A** events are not stored indefinitely; **C** the default is about one hour, not 30 days, and this is retention, not RBAC; **D** events are not durably written to node disk.

questions.stem: Your container app's environment is integrated with a Log Analytics workspace. Your application writes diagnostic messages to stdout and stderr, and you want to query those application logs with Kusto. Which table should you query?

options.text: ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL
AzureActivity
ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL
AppRequests

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Console logs come from the stdout and stderr of the containers in your app, and you query them in the ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL table. Why the others are wrong: **A** ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL holds service-generated messages such as revision provisioning, not your app's stdout/stderr; **B** AzureActivity records control-plane operations, not container output; **D** AppRequests is an Application Insights table, not the Container Apps console log table.

questions.stem: You are triaging an Azure Container Apps issue where the service reports problems provisioning a revision. Which two facts about Container Apps log types are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: System logs (ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL) carry service messages such as 'Creating a new revision' and 'Error provisioning revision'
Console logs capture the container's stdout and stderr output
System logs contain your application's stdout output
Console logs are emitted only by the ingress layer, not the containers

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** System logs are generated by the Container Apps service and include revision-provisioning messages and errors, while console logs capture stdout/stderr from your containers and Dapr sidecars. Why the others are wrong: **C** application stdout goes to console logs, not system logs; **D** console logs come from the containers themselves, whereas the ingress layer emits separate HTTP logs.

questions.stem: A web Service you deployed to AKS is unreachable from the internet. Arrange these troubleshooting steps into the correct end-to-end order, from confirming the workload is healthy to confirming external reachability.

options.text: Run kubectl get pods to confirm the application pods are Running and Ready
Run kubectl describe pod on any pod that is not Ready to read its events
Run kubectl get service and confirm the Service has an assigned EXTERNAL-IP
Browse to http://<external-ip> to confirm the app responds over the internet

questions.explanation: Troubleshoot connectivity from the inside out. First run kubectl get pods (A) to confirm the workload pods are Running and Ready. If a pod is not Ready, kubectl describe pod (B) surfaces the events explaining why. Next, kubectl get service (C) verifies the LoadBalancer Service obtained an EXTERNAL-IP rather than staying <pending>. Finally, browsing to http://<external-ip> (D) confirms end-to-end external reachability. This bottom-up order isolates the failure layer by layer before testing the public endpoint.

questions.stem: Your ASP.NET Core service uses the Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL .NET SDK (Microsoft.Azure.Cosmos). To follow Microsoft's connection guidance and avoid socket exhaustion under load, how should you manage the CosmosClient?

options.text: Create a new CosmosClient inside every request handler and dispose it before returning
Create one CosmosClient instance and reuse it as a singleton for the lifetime of the application
Create a separate CosmosClient for each logical partition key you read
Wrap each CreateItemAsync call in its own short-lived CosmosClient using block

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** CosmosClient is thread-safe, manages its own connection pool, and is designed to be instantiated once and reused as a singleton for the app's lifetime. Why the others are wrong: **A** per-request clients exhaust sockets and add connection-warmup latency; **C** clients are account/endpoint-scoped, not partition-scoped, so one per partition is meaningless overhead; **D** a short-lived client per write recreates the connection pool each call.

questions.stem: A retrieval service knows both the item id and the partition key value of a document it needs from a Cosmos DB for NoSQL container. Which .NET SDK call retrieves that single document with the lowest RU cost?

options.text: container.GetItemQueryIterator<T>("SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.id = @id")
container.GetItemLinqQueryable<T>().Where(x => x.Id == id)
container.ReadItemAsync<T>(id, new PartitionKey(pkValue))
database.ReadItemAsync<T>(id) on the parent database

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A point read with ReadItemAsync, supplying both id and the PartitionKey, fetches exactly one document and is the cheapest possible read (about 1 RU for a 1 KB item). Why the others are wrong: **A** a query is processed by the query engine and costs more RUs than a point read; **B** a LINQ query also compiles to a SQL query, not a point read; **D** point reads are issued on a Container, not on Database.

questions.stem: You run a category filter query with the Cosmos DB for NoSQL .NET SDK and need to page through all matching items. Which pattern correctly drains every page from the FeedIterator?

options.text: while (feed.HasMoreResults) { FeedResponse<T> page = await feed.ReadNextAsync(); /* process page */ }
var all = await feed.ReadAllAsync(); // returns every item in one call
foreach (T item in feed) { /* iterator is synchronous and self-paging */ }
for (int i = 0; i < feed.PageCount; i++) await feed.ReadPageAsync(i);

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A query returns a FeedIterator; you loop while HasMoreResults is true and call ReadNextAsync to fetch each page (a FeedResponse) until the iterator is drained. Why the others are wrong: **B** there is no ReadAllAsync that returns the full result set in one call; **C** FeedIterator is not a synchronous IEnumerable you can foreach directly; **D** there is no PageCount/ReadPageAsync(index) API on the iterator.

questions.stem: To prevent SQL/NoSQL injection when building a query whose category value comes from user input, how should you construct the query with the Cosmos DB for NoSQL .NET SDK?

options.text: String-concatenate the value directly into the SELECT statement before sending it
Use string.Format to splice the value into the WHERE clause
URL-encode the value and append it to the query text
Build a QueryDefinition with a @category placeholder and bind the value using .WithParameter("@category", value)

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** QueryDefinition supports parameterized queries: you reference a named placeholder like @category in the text and bind the value with WithParameter, which keeps user input as data, not executable query text. Why the others are wrong: **A** and **B** concatenation/string.Format splice raw input into the query, the classic injection vector; **C** encoding does not separate code from data and still allows injection.

questions.stem: After each operation, your team wants to log how many request units a Cosmos DB for NoSQL call consumed so they can spot expensive queries. Which member of the .NET SDK response exposes the RU charge?

options.text: response.StatusCode converted to an RU value
response.RequestCharge on the ItemResponse or FeedResponse
response.ActivityId, which encodes the RU cost
response.ETag, which increments by the RUs used

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Every ItemResponse and FeedResponse exposes a RequestCharge property reporting the RUs consumed by that operation, which you log to find costly calls. Why the others are wrong: **A** StatusCode reports success/failure (for example 200 or 429), not cost; **C** ActivityId is a diagnostic correlation id, not an RU figure; **D** ETag is a concurrency token for optimistic concurrency, unrelated to RU consumption.

questions.stem: A Cosmos DB for NoSQL container stores large telemetry documents, but queries only ever filter on a few scalar properties. Writes are consuming far more RUs than expected. Which indexing change most directly lowers the RU charge of writes while preserving those queries?

options.text: Switch indexingMode to none so the container is never indexed
Add a composite index covering every property in the document
Keep indexingMode consistent, include only the queried paths, and exclude the rest (or include /* and exclude the unused subtrees)
Increase the provisioned RU/s so writes no longer throttle

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** By default every path is indexed, so trimming the indexed paths to just the queried ones (via included/excluded paths) cuts the index-maintenance work on each write, lowering write RU charge while the filter queries still use their indexes. Why the others are wrong: **A** none disables all indexing and breaks the filter queries (they would full-scan); **B** indexing more paths raises write cost; **D** more RU/s hides the cost, it does not reduce per-write RUs.

questions.stem: A frequent query orders results by two properties: ORDER BY c.lastName ASC, c.firstName ASC. It is slow and RU-heavy. What must you add to the indexing policy to support it?

options.text: Separate single range indexes on lastName and firstName
A composite index on (lastName ASC, firstName ASC)
A spatial index covering both properties
Set indexingMode to lazy so the sort is precomputed

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An ORDER BY on two or more properties requires a composite index whose paths and sort directions match the clause, so (lastName ASC, firstName ASC) serves this query. Why the others are wrong: **A** independent range indexes cannot satisfy a multi-property ORDER BY; **C** spatial indexes are for geospatial functions, not multi-key sorts; **D** lazy mode lowers index priority and yields incomplete results, it is not for sorting and is not allowed for queried containers.

questions.stem: In a Cosmos DB for NoSQL indexing policy, a property path matches both a more specific included path and a less specific excluded path. Which rule determines whether that path is indexed?

options.text: Excluded paths always win over included paths regardless of precision
Included paths always win over excluded paths regardless of precision
The path listed first in the JSON document takes precedence
The more precise (deeper/more specific) path takes precedence over the less precise one

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** When included and excluded paths conflict, Cosmos DB applies the more precise path; for example an included /food/ingredients/nutrition/* overrides a broader excluded /food/ingredients/*. Why the others are wrong: **A** and **B** neither include nor exclude wins unconditionally, precision decides; **C** ordering of entries in the JSON does not affect precedence, the specificity of the path does.

questions.stem: When you create a new Azure Cosmos DB account and do not change any consistency setting, which consistency level applies by default to reads and queries?

options.text: Strong
Eventual
Session
Bounded staleness

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Session is the default consistency level for a new account; it provides read-your-writes and write-follows-reads guarantees within a client session at performance comparable to eventual consistency. Why the others are wrong: **A** strong is the strongest but is opt-in and costs more; **B** eventual is the weakest and not the default; **D** bounded staleness is configurable but is not the out-of-the-box default.

questions.stem: A read-heavy AI feature on Cosmos DB for NoSQL is RU-constrained. Switching the account from strong to session consistency is acceptable for the workload. What read-side effect on request units does this change have?

options.text: Read RU cost roughly halves, because session uses single-replica reads while strong (and bounded staleness) read from two replicas
Read RU cost roughly doubles, because weaker consistency requires more replicas to be consulted
Read RU cost is unchanged; consistency level never affects RU charge
Write RU cost halves, but reads are unaffected

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Strong and bounded staleness perform a local-minority read from two replicas, costing about twice the RUs of session, consistent prefix, and eventual, which read from a single replica; so moving to session roughly halves read RU. Why the others are wrong: **B** weaker consistency consults fewer replicas, not more; **C** consistency does affect read RU; **D** write RU is identical across consistency levels, the savings are on reads.

questions.stem: An architecture requires multiple write regions (active-active) for a Cosmos DB account. Which consistency level is NOT available with multiple write regions?

options.text: Session
Strong
Consistent prefix
Eventual

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Accounts with multiple write regions cannot use strong consistency, because a distributed multi-master system cannot guarantee an RPO and RTO of zero, and strong would also force writes to commit to every region. Why the others are wrong: **A**, **C**, and **D** session, consistent prefix, and eventual are all supported with multiple write regions and replicate to a local majority before async cross-region replication.

questions.stem: Before you can store embeddings and run vector similarity search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, what must you do at the account level?

options.text: Switch the account API from NoSQL to the MongoDB vCore API
Set the default consistency level to strong
Enable the Vector Search for NoSQL API feature (capability EnableNoSQLVectorSearch) on the account
Provision a dedicated gateway and enable autoscale

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Vector search on the NoSQL API is an account-level feature you must opt into, either in the portal under Features or via the CLI capability EnableNoSQLVectorSearch, before defining a vector policy. Why the others are wrong: **A** vector search is supported on the NoSQL API itself, no API switch is required; **B** consistency level is unrelated to enabling vector search; **D** a dedicated gateway and autoscale do not enable the vector capability.

questions.stem: In a Cosmos DB for NoSQL query, which system function computes the similarity/distance between a stored embedding property and a query vector for semantic retrieval?

options.text: ST_DISTANCE(c.contentVector, @queryVector)
VectorDistance(c.contentVector, @queryVector)
COSINE_SIMILARITY(c.contentVector, @queryVector)
DOT(c.contentVector, @queryVector)

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** VectorDistance is the built-in system function for vector similarity; you use it in the SELECT projection and the ORDER BY to rank items by closeness to the query vector. Why the others are wrong: **A** ST_DISTANCE is a geospatial function for points/geometries, not embeddings; **C** and **D** COSINE_SIMILARITY and DOT are not the NoSQL function names, the distance metric (cosine, dot product, euclidean) is set in the vector policy and applied by VectorDistance.

questions.stem: You store 1536-dimension embeddings from an Azure OpenAI model and need an exact (100% recall) nearest-neighbor search over a small, filtered set of vectors. The flat vector index supports at most 505 dimensions. Which vector index type fits 1536 dimensions while still doing a brute-force (exact-style) search?

options.text: flat
diskANN
quantizedFlat
A standard range index on the vector path

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** quantizedFlat performs a brute-force search like flat but supports up to 4096 dimensions and compresses (quantizes) vectors, so it handles 1536-dim embeddings with near-exact recall, ideal for small, filtered vector sets. Why the others are wrong: **A** flat is brute-force but caps at 505 dimensions, too few for 1536; **B** diskANN is approximate (ANN), not exact; **D** a range index does not perform vector similarity search at all.

questions.stem: You are writing a Cosmos DB for NoSQL query to return the 10 most semantically similar documents to a query embedding. Which two practices does Microsoft recommend for an efficient vector search query? (Select two.)

options.text: Include a TOP N clause (for example, SELECT TOP 10) in the query
Order results by VectorDistance(...) so the closest items rank first
Omit any ORDER BY so the engine returns every candidate vector
Sort the results client-side after retrieving the entire container

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Microsoft advises always using a TOP N in the SELECT so the search does not return more rows than needed, and ordering by VectorDistance so the most similar items come first; together they cut RU and latency. Why the others are wrong: **C** omitting ORDER BY returns unranked, far more results and raises cost; **D** pulling the whole container to sort client-side is the anti-pattern these guidelines exist to prevent.

questions.stem: You deploy the Cosmos DB for NoSQL change feed processor on three compute instances so that one deployment unit shares the work of reading the monitored container. Which two configuration requirements let those instances load-balance the leases? (Select two.)

options.text: All instances use the same lease container configuration
All instances use the same processorName
Every instance uses the same instance name set via WithInstanceName
Each instance points at a different monitored (source) container

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Instances in one deployment unit balance leases only when they share the same lease container configuration and the same processorName; the processor then distributes leases across them. Why the others are wrong: **C** instance names must be unique per instance (WithInstanceName), identical names break the distribution; **D** they must all monitor the same source container, different containers are different workloads, not a shared unit.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps to build and start a Cosmos DB for NoSQL change feed processor (latest version mode) in the correct order using the .NET SDK builder.

options.text: Call GetChangeFeedProcessorBuilder on the monitored container, passing the processorName and the onChanges delegate
Chain WithInstanceName to set this compute instance's unique name
Chain WithLeaseContainer to supply the lease container, then call Build()
Call StartAsync on the resulting processor to begin reading changes

questions.explanation: The builder pattern starts on the monitored container: GetChangeFeedProcessorBuilder takes the processorName and the delegate that handles each batch (A). You then set this instance's unique identity with WithInstanceName (B), point the processor at the lease container that stores checkpoint/continuation state with WithLeaseContainer and call Build() to materialize it (C), and finally StartAsync begins listening for changes (D). The lease container must be configured before Build, and Build must precede StartAsync.

questions.stem: You want to add vector similarity search to an Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server by enabling the pgvector capability. After allowlisting it in azure.extensions, which SQL statement enables it in the connected database?

options.text: CREATE EXTENSION vector;
CREATE EXTENSION pgvector;
INSTALL EXTENSION vector;
ALTER SYSTEM SET shared_preload_libraries = 'pgvector';

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Although the community calls it pgvector, the binary and extension are named simply `vector`, so you enable it with CREATE EXTENSION vector;. Why the others are wrong: **B** `pgvector` is not the registered extension name and CREATE EXTENSION fails; **C** INSTALL EXTENSION is not valid PostgreSQL syntax; **D** pgvector is enabled per database with CREATE EXTENSION, not via shared_preload_libraries.

questions.stem: Your RAG pipeline generates 1536-dimension embeddings from Azure OpenAI text-embedding-3-small. You need a column in an Azure Database for PostgreSQL table to store each embedding so it can later be indexed for similarity search. Which column definition should you use?

options.text: embedding float8[]
embedding vector(1536)
embedding jsonb
embedding bytea

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The pgvector `vector(n)` type stores a fixed-dimension embedding; declaring vector(1536) lets you later build an HNSW or IVFFlat index. Why the others are wrong: **A** a float8[] array supports neither the distance operators nor vector indexes; **C** jsonb stores the numbers but cannot be indexed by pgvector or queried with <=>; **D** bytea is opaque binary with no vector operators or indexing.

questions.stem: In a semantic retrieval query against Azure Database for PostgreSQL, you must rank stored embeddings by cosine distance to a query vector. Which pgvector operator computes cosine distance?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** In pgvector the `<=>` operator returns cosine distance, ideal for semantic similarity ranking. Why the others are wrong: **A** `<->` returns Euclidean (L2) distance, not cosine; **B** `<#>` returns the negative inner product; **D** `<@>` is not a pgvector distance operator.

questions.stem: You build an IVFFlat index for cosine similarity on the embedding column in Azure Database for PostgreSQL, but EXPLAIN shows queries using the <=> operator still perform a sequential scan. The index was created with vector_l2_ops. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The index operator class does not match the query operator; a cosine query needs an index built with vector_cosine_ops.
IVFFlat indexes can only be used with the <-> operator regardless of operator class.
Cosine distance cannot be indexed in pgvector, only Euclidean distance can.
The lists parameter must equal the table row count for the planner to use the index.

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The planner only uses a vector index whose operator class matches the query operator, so a `<=>` (cosine) query requires an index built with vector_cosine_ops, not vector_l2_ops. Why the others are wrong: **B** IVFFlat works with <=>, <->, or <#> depending on the operator class; **C** cosine is fully indexable via vector_cosine_ops; **D** setting probes/lists to the full count forces a brute-force scan, the opposite of using the index.

questions.stem: An approximate nearest-neighbor query on an HNSW index in Azure Database for PostgreSQL is returning too few relevant results (low recall). You want to widen the search at query time without rebuilding the index. Which runtime setting should you increase?

options.text: SET ivfflat.probes to a higher value
SET hnsw.ef_search to a value larger than the default of 40
Increase the m parameter on the existing index
Increase ef_construction on the existing index

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** `hnsw.ef_search` (default 40) sizes the dynamic candidate list at query time; raising it improves recall at some cost to speed, with no rebuild. Why the others are wrong: **A** ivfflat.probes only affects IVFFlat indexes, not HNSW; **C** `m` is a build-time HNSW parameter and changing it requires recreating the index; **D** `ef_construction` is also build-time and cannot be altered on an existing index.

questions.stem: You are loading 5 million OpenAI embeddings into a new Azure Database for PostgreSQL table and will serve approximate similarity searches. To get both a faster index build and the best speed-recall tradeoff, what should you do?

options.text: Bulk-load all rows first, then create the vector index on the populated table.
Create the HNSW index on the empty table first, then insert the rows one at a time.
Insert rows in small batches and rebuild the index after every batch.
Skip indexing entirely because exact search is always faster at this scale.

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Microsoft guidance is to load data before indexing; building the index once on a populated table is faster and produces a more optimal layout. Why the others are wrong: **B** inserting row-by-row after creating the index is far slower and yields a worse layout; **C** rebuilding after every batch wastes work and time; **D** without an index pgvector does an exact scan with perfect recall but poor performance at millions of rows.

questions.stem: Your embeddings from Azure OpenAI are normalized to unit length. You want the best query performance for similarity search on Azure Database for PostgreSQL. Which distance operator does Microsoft recommend for normalized vectors?

options.text: Euclidean distance (<->)
Cosine distance (<=>)
Taxicab/L1 distance (l1_distance)
Inner product (<#>)

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** When vectors are normalized to length 1 (like OpenAI embeddings), Microsoft recommends inner product `<#>` for best performance because it avoids the extra normalization work cosine requires. Why the others are wrong: **A** Euclidean is valid but not the recommended fastest choice for normalized vectors; **B** cosine gives equivalent ranking on unit vectors but does redundant normalization; **C** L1 is a different metric not recommended here.

questions.stem: Your RAG application stores document embeddings plus a tenant_id and a category column in Azure Database for PostgreSQL. Most searches are filtered to a single high-traffic tenant. To make those filtered similarity searches efficient, which approach best leverages pgvector?

options.text: Create a partial vector index with a WHERE clause matching the tenant, and query using the same predicate form.
Store every tenant's embeddings in one unindexed column and filter only in application code after retrieval.
Drop all metadata columns so the planner is forced to use the vector index.
Use ivfflat.probes = 1 so only the closest list is searched for that tenant.

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A partial vector index (CREATE INDEX ... WHERE tenant_id = ...) indexes only that subset, so it is smaller and faster, but the query predicate must match the index form for the planner to use it. Why the others are wrong: **B** post-filtering in app code still scans and ranks all tenants' vectors; **C** dropping metadata loses needed filtering and does not help the index; **D** probes=1 reduces recall and does not implement metadata filtering.

questions.stem: A data scientist tries to create an IVFFlat index on a column declared as embedding vector (no dimension) in Azure Database for PostgreSQL and receives an error. What must change so the column can be indexed?

options.text: Increase max_parallel_maintenance_workers before creating the index.
Declare the column with a fixed dimension, for example vector(768), because only dimensioned vector columns can be indexed.
Convert the column to jsonb and index it with a GIN index instead.
Add more than 2000 dimensions so the index has enough entries to build.

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** pgvector can only index a column that has dimensions defined; indexing a bare `vector` column raises 'column does not have dimensions', so you must declare e.g. vector(768). Why the others are wrong: **A** worker settings affect build speed, not the missing-dimension error; **C** jsonb/GIN does not provide vector similarity search; **D** columns over 2000 dimensions cannot be indexed at all, which is the opposite requirement.

questions.stem: You are comparing IVFFlat and HNSW indexes for a vector workload on Azure Database for PostgreSQL. Which two statements accurately describe HNSW relative to IVFFlat? (Select two.)

options.text: HNSW builds faster and uses less memory than IVFFlat.
HNSW generally offers a better speed-recall tradeoff than IVFFlat.
HNSW requires the lists parameter to partition the dataset before building.
HNSW can be created on an empty table because it has no training step.

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, D):** HNSW gives a better speed-recall tradeoff and, unlike IVFFlat's k-means training, has no training step so it can be built on an empty table. Why the others are wrong: **A** is reversed—IVFFlat builds faster and uses less memory, while HNSW costs more time and memory; **C** the `lists` option applies only to IVFFlat, not HNSW.

questions.stem: Similarity queries on a large vector table in Azure Database for PostgreSQL show high latency, and monitoring indicates the index and working set spill out of memory, causing heavy disk reads. Which configuration change most directly addresses vector query latency for this workload?

options.text: Scale the server to a compute tier with more memory so the index and hot vectors fit in RAM.
Lower hnsw.ef_search to 1 to read fewer candidates from disk.
Drop the vector index so every query becomes an in-memory exact scan.
Switch the column from vector to text to reduce its storage footprint.

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Vector search is fastest when the index and frequently accessed vectors fit in memory; provisioning more memory (compute/memory sizing for vector workloads) removes the disk-read bottleneck. Why the others are wrong: **B** ef_search=1 cuts recall sharply and does not solve memory pressure; **C** an exact scan over millions of rows is slower, not faster, and still must read all data; **D** storing embeddings as text breaks vector operators and indexing entirely.

questions.stem: A Python service using a connection-per-request pattern against Azure Database for PostgreSQL spends most of its time establishing new TCP and TLS connections, hurting throughput under load. Which change best optimizes connection overhead?

options.text: Open a brand-new connection for every query to avoid stale sockets.
Disable TLS so connections complete faster.
Use a connection pool (such as PgBouncer or a client-side pool) to reuse established connections across requests.
Move all reads to client-side memory and stop querying the database.

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Reusing connections through a pool eliminates repeated TCP/TLS setup per request, the standard way to optimize throughput and latency for high-concurrency PostgreSQL apps. Why the others are wrong: **A** a fresh connection per query is exactly the overhead causing the problem; **B** disabling TLS removes encryption and is not an acceptable optimization on Azure; **D** caching everything client-side abandons the database rather than optimizing its connections.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps to implement a RAG retrieval store with pgvector on Azure Database for PostgreSQL, from first to last.

options.text: Enable the extension with CREATE EXTENSION vector;
Create a table with a vector(n) embedding column sized to the model's dimensions
Generate embeddings with Azure OpenAI and bulk-insert them with their source text and metadata
Create an HNSW or IVFFlat index, then run ORDER BY embedding <=> $query LIMIT k to retrieve nearest chunks

questions.explanation: The correct order is A, B, C, D. First enable the extension (CREATE EXTENSION vector) so the vector type exists. Next define the table with a dimensioned vector(n) column matching the embedding model. Then generate embeddings in Azure OpenAI and bulk-load them with text and metadata—loading before indexing yields a faster, better index. Finally create the ANN index and query with the cosine operator and LIMIT k to return the nearest chunks for grounding. Indexing after the bulk load and before serving queries is what makes retrieval both correct and fast.

questions.stem: You need to add vector similarity search to a cache so it can act as a vector database for a semantic answer engine. Which Azure Managed Redis module provides KNN vector search over stored embeddings?

options.text: RediSearch
RedisBloom
RedisTimeSeries
RedisJSON

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** RediSearch adds the real-time search engine that performs vector similarity (KNN) queries, letting Azure Managed Redis serve as a vector database. Why the others are wrong: **B** RedisBloom provides probabilistic structures (bloom/cuckoo filters, count-min, top-k), not vector search; **C** RedisTimeSeries handles time-series data; **D** RedisJSON stores and queries JSON and pairs with RediSearch for indexing but does not itself perform vector search.

questions.stem: You enable the RediSearch module on a new Azure Managed Redis instance to host a vector index. Which configuration does RediSearch require?

options.text: The OSS clustering policy and the allkeys-lru eviction policy.
The Basic tier with volatile-ttl eviction.
The Enterprise clustering policy and the NoEviction eviction policy.
Active geo-replication enabled before any keys are written.

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Microsoft documents that RediSearch requires the Enterprise clustering policy and the NoEviction eviction policy so indexed data is not evicted under memory pressure. Why the others are wrong: **A** OSS clustering with an LRU eviction policy is not the supported configuration for RediSearch; **B** the Basic tier does not support modules at all; **D** active geo-replication is optional (RediSearch and RedisJSON can use it) and is not a prerequisite for the module.

questions.stem: On Azure Managed Redis with RediSearch, you must return the exact nearest neighbors for a small benchmark dataset, prioritizing maximum precision over speed. Which vector index type should you choose?

options.text: HNSW, which trades precision for speed using approximate nearest neighbor search.
IVFFlat, the default approximate index in RediSearch.
A bloom filter index over the embedding field.
FLAT, which performs an exhaustive brute-force KNN search for exact results.

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** RediSearch's FLAT index is a brute-force method that performs exact KNN, giving the highest precision at higher compute cost—appropriate for a small benchmark. Why the others are wrong: **A** HNSW is the approximate (ANN) method that trades precision for speed; **B** RediSearch's approximate option is HNSW, not IVFFlat; **C** a bloom filter is a probabilistic set-membership structure, not a vector index.

questions.stem: You implement a cache-aside pattern with Azure Managed Redis in front of Azure Database for PostgreSQL and must keep cached entries fresh. Which two techniques correctly manage cached data freshness? (Select two.)

options.text: Cache every value permanently with no expiration to maximize hit rate.
Set a time-to-live (TTL) on keys so stale entries expire automatically.
On a write to the source database, invalidate or refresh the corresponding cache key.
Disable persistence so all keys are deleted on each restart instead of expiring.

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, C):** Applying a TTL expires stale entries automatically, and invalidating or refreshing the key on a source write keeps the cache consistent—the core of cache-aside. Why the others are wrong: **A** caching forever serves stale data once the source changes; **D** relying on restarts to clear keys is not a freshness strategy and loses unrelated cached data.

questions.stem: You want to store each document as a single Redis entry containing the embedding plus structured metadata (title, tags), then run vector search with metadata filters on Azure Managed Redis. Which combination of modules and data structure best supports this?

options.text: Store documents only as plain strings and parse them in the client for every query.
Store documents as JSON using RedisJSON and index the vector and metadata fields with RediSearch for hybrid filtered search.
Use RedisTimeSeries to hold the embeddings and filter by timestamp.
Use RedisBloom to store embeddings and approximate metadata membership.

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** RedisJSON stores document-like JSON, and RediSearch can index both the vector field and JSON metadata to perform hybrid (filtered) vector search—the two modules are designed to work together. Why the others are wrong: **A** plain strings cannot be indexed for vector or field search; **C** RedisTimeSeries is for time-series data, not embeddings with metadata; **D** RedisBloom only answers probabilistic set membership and cannot store embeddings or run vector search.

questions.stem: Your AI scoring service publishes inference requests to an Azure Service Bus queue, and a pool of worker instances reads them so spikes in traffic don't overwhelm the back end. Each request must be processed by exactly one worker, and a slow worker must not let another worker grab the same request. Which receive mode should the workers use?

options.text: PeekLock, so the message is locked exclusively until the worker calls Complete
ReceiveAndDelete, so the message is removed from the queue the instant it is delivered
A topic subscription, so every worker receives its own copy of each request
Presettled AMQP transfers, so no acknowledgment round trip is required

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** PeekLock locks the message exclusively until the worker calls Complete, so competing receivers can't take it while one processes it, and unsettled work is redelivered. Why the others are wrong: **B** ReceiveAndDelete settles on delivery, so a crash mid-processing loses the request; **C** a subscription copies the message to every subscriber, breaking once-per-worker; **D** presettled transfers describe sending, not competing-consumer receive.

questions.stem: A worker reading from a Service Bus queue under PeekLock encounters a transient downstream error and wants the same message redelivered immediately so it can retry. Which settlement call should it make?

options.text: Complete the message
Dead-letter the message
Abandon the message
Defer the message

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Abandon releases the lock instantly so the message returns to the front of the queue for redelivery; it also increments the delivery count. Why the others are wrong: **A** Complete removes the message as successfully processed, so no retry occurs; **B** dead-lettering moves the message to the DLQ and is for messages that won't succeed on retry; **D** deferral sets the message aside and requires the receiver to later fetch it by sequence number, not an immediate redelivery.

questions.stem: Messages in a Service Bus queue keep landing in the dead-letter queue with the reason code MaxDeliveryCountExceeded, even though the downstream service is healthy. Investigation shows workers routinely take longer than the lock duration to finish, so locks expire mid-processing. What is the MOST direct fix?

options.text: Increase the queue's MaxDeliveryCount to a very large value so messages are never dead-lettered
Switch the receivers to ReceiveAndDelete mode to eliminate lock expiration
Renew the message lock (or set a longer lock duration) so it doesn't expire before processing completes
Enable duplicate detection on the queue

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** When a lock expires the message unlocks and the delivery count increments; enough expirations exceed MaxDeliveryCount and dead-letter it. Renewing the lock or raising the lock duration (max 5 minutes) keeps it held. Why the others are wrong: **A** a huge MaxDeliveryCount only delays repeated failed redeliveries; **B** ReceiveAndDelete trades the problem for message loss; **D** duplicate detection suppresses duplicate sends, unrelated to lock expiry.

questions.stem: Using the Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus .NET library, you need a receiver that reads messages from a queue's dead-letter queue so an operator can inspect failed AI jobs. How should you create the receiver?

options.text: Create a receiver and set ServiceBusReceiverOptions.SubQueue to SubQueue.DeadLetter
Append "/$deadletterqueue" to the queue name and pass that string as the queue name to CreateReceiver
Create a separate queue named "<queue>-deadletter" and point the receiver at it
Call CreateReceiver with ReceiveMode set to ReceiveAndDelete

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** With the modern Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus library you target the DLQ by setting ServiceBusReceiverOptions.SubQueue to SubQueue.DeadLetter; the library builds the sub-queue path for you. Why the others are wrong: **B** the /$deadletterqueue path syntax is for CLI/REST/tools, not the SDK's queue-name argument; **C** the DLQ is a system sub-queue that can't be created or deleted independently; **D** ReceiveMode controls settlement behavior, not which (sub-)entity is read.

questions.stem: Which conditions cause Azure Service Bus to automatically move a message to the dead-letter queue without the application explicitly dead-lettering it? (Select two.)

options.text: The message's time-to-live expires while dead-lettering on expiration is enabled
A receiver successfully calls Complete on the message
The delivery count exceeds the entity's MaxDeliveryCount
The message is deferred by the receiver for later retrieval

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Service Bus auto-dead-letters when a message's TTL expires with dead-letter-on-expiration enabled (TTLExpiredException) and when delivery attempts exceed MaxDeliveryCount (MaxDeliveryCountExceeded). Why the others are wrong: **B** Complete settles a message as processed and removes it, the opposite of dead-lettering; **D** deferral sets a message aside in the main entity for later fetch and never moves it to the DLQ.

questions.stem: An operator notices the dead-letter queue for a subscription keeps growing and asks how messages are removed from it. Which statement about the Service Bus dead-letter queue is correct?

options.text: Messages in the DLQ expire automatically based on the entity's time-to-live setting
Messages remain in the DLQ until a receiver explicitly retrieves and completes them
The DLQ is purged automatically every 14 days by the messaging engine
Messages can be moved from one DLQ to another DLQ for archival

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The DLQ has no automatic cleanup; TTL isn't observed there, so messages stay until a receiver explicitly receives and completes (or otherwise settles) them. Why the others are wrong: **A** time-to-live is specifically not applied to messages already in the DLQ; **C** there is no 14-day automatic purge of the DLQ; **D** you can't dead-letter a message that is already in a dead-letter queue, so DLQ-to-DLQ moves aren't possible.

questions.stem: An AI pipeline publishes document-processed events to a single Service Bus topic. The billing service should receive only events where the custom property department equals "finance", while the audit service receives every event. What is the correct way to implement this routing?

options.text: Create two topics and have the publisher decide at send time which topic each event goes to
Create two subscriptions on the topic; apply a SQL/correlation filter on the billing subscription and the default TrueFilter on the audit subscription
Create a single subscription and have both services compete for messages from it
Use a single queue and rely on message sessions to separate finance messages from the rest

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Each topic subscription is independent and can carry a filter rule; a SQL/correlation filter (department = 'finance') selects billing's copies, while the audit subscription's default true filter gets all messages. Why the others are wrong: **A** two topics push routing into the publisher, losing pub/sub fan-out; **C** one shared subscription makes the services compete, so neither gets its required set; **D** sessions enforce FIFO grouping, not content routing.

questions.stem: You enable autoforwarding to chain Service Bus entities so messages flow through several queues before reaching a processor. To prevent infinite forwarding loops, Service Bus limits how many hops a message may take and dead-letters it if the limit is exceeded. What is that maximum number of hops?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A message that passes through more than four chained queues or topics is dead-lettered with reason MaxTransferHopCountExceeded; the documented limit is 4 hops. Why the others are wrong: **B** 10 is the default MaxDeliveryCount for redelivery attempts, not the autoforward hop limit; **C** a single hop would defeat the purpose of chaining entities; **D** 32 is not a Service Bus autoforwarding limit.

questions.stem: Your blob-upload pipeline triggers AI enrichment through Azure Event Grid. The handler endpoint occasionally returns HTTP 503 (Service Unavailable) during deployments. What does Event Grid do with an event when the subscriber returns 503?

options.text: It immediately dead-letters the event because 5xx codes indicate permanent failure
It drops the event silently with no retry
It retries delivery using an exponential backoff schedule until the event is accepted or the retry policy limit is reached
It marks the subscription as failed and stops delivering all future events to it

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** 503 is transient, so Event Grid retries with exponential backoff (10s, 30s, 1m, and so on) until the event is acknowledged or the retry policy's max-attempts/TTL limit is hit. Why the others are wrong: **A** only codes such as 400 and 413 trigger immediate dead-lettering, not 503; **B** events drop only after retries are exhausted with no dead-letter set; **D** Event Grid doesn't permanently disable a subscription over transient errors.

questions.stem: An Event Grid subscription delivers to a webhook that returns HTTP 400 (Bad Request) because the handler can't parse the payload schema. No dead-letter destination is configured. What happens to the event?

options.text: Event Grid retries with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours
Event Grid does not retry and drops the event because no dead-letter location is configured
Event Grid stores the event in its own internal queue until the handler is fixed
Event Grid returns the event to the publisher for resubmission

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A 400 is treated as a non-retryable delivery failure; Event Grid immediately stops trying and, with no dead-letter destination set, drops the event. Why the others are wrong: **A** 400 is explicitly excluded from the retry/backoff schedule; **C** Event Grid doesn't hold undelivered events in an internal queue for the subscriber, undelivered events go to a dead-letter blob container only if one is configured; **D** there is no return-to-publisher mechanism.

questions.stem: You must configure Event Grid so that undelivered events are not lost when a subscriber is unavailable past the retry window. Where does Event Grid place dead-lettered events?

options.text: In a secondary Event Grid topic created automatically for the subscription
In a blob container in an Azure Storage account that you specify on the event subscription
In the dead-letter sub-queue of the source resource
In an Azure Service Bus queue that Event Grid provisions for you

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Event Grid dead-lettering writes undelivered events to a blob container in a Storage account you specify on the subscription; you then pull events from it to reconcile. Why the others are wrong: **A** Event Grid doesn't auto-create a secondary topic for dead letters; **C** dead-letter sub-queues are a Service Bus concept, not Event Grid's destination; **D** the dead-letter location is specifically Azure Storage blob and isn't auto-provisioned.

questions.stem: On an Event Grid subscription you set the retry policy to a maximum of 10 delivery attempts and an event time-to-live (TTL) of 30 minutes. Given Event Grid's exponential backoff schedule, only about 6 attempts occur within 30 minutes. After how long, or how many attempts, will an undelivered event be dead-lettered?

options.text: After 10 attempts, because max attempts always takes precedence over TTL
After 30 minutes, because Event Grid stops at whichever limit (TTL or max attempts) is reached first
After 24 hours, the default maximum event lifetime
Only when both 10 attempts and 30 minutes have elapsed

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Event Grid stops delivery at the first limit to expire. Here the 30-minute TTL is reached after ~6 backoff attempts, before the 10-attempt cap, so the event is dead-lettered at 30 minutes and the max-attempts setting has no effect. Why the others are wrong: **A** max attempts does not override TTL, whichever comes first wins; **C** 24 hours/1440 minutes is the default TTL, but you overrode it to 30 minutes; **D** the policy uses first-to-expire, not both-must-be-met.

questions.stem: A custom application publishes events to an Event Grid custom topic. A handler should receive only events whose data.priority value is greater than 7. Which filtering approach should you configure on the event subscription?

options.text: An advanced filter with operatorType NumberGreaterThan, key data.priority, and value 7
A subjectBeginsWith filter set to "7"
An includedEventTypes filter listing the priority levels above 7
A subjectEndsWith filter set to data.priority

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Advanced filters compare values inside the event using an operator, a key (dot-notation into data), and a value, so NumberGreaterThan on data.priority with value 7 matches priorities above 7. Why the others are wrong: **B** subjectBeginsWith does prefix string matching on the subject, not numeric comparison; **C** includedEventTypes filters by eventType strings, not numeric data; **D** subjectEndsWith is a string-suffix match and can't compare data.priority numerically.

questions.stem: You are designing advanced filtering for an Event Grid subscription that routes AI model events. Which statements about Event Grid advanced filtering are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: A subscription may define at most 25 advanced filters, with a total of 25 filter values across all of them
When you specify multiple different advanced filters, they are combined with an AND, so every filter must match
Listing multiple values within a single filter requires all of those values to match (an AND)
Advanced filters can compare only the subject string and cannot reference fields in the event data

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Advanced filtering is capped at 25 filters and 25 filter values per subscription, and multiple distinct filters are AND-ed so each condition must be satisfied. Why the others are wrong: **C** multiple values inside one filter are OR-ed, the key need match only one of them; **D** advanced filters explicitly support keys into event data via dot notation (for example data.priority), not just the subject.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps to set up an event-driven workflow that publishes custom application events through Azure Event Grid and routes only matching events to a webhook handler. Order the steps from first to last.

options.text: Create an Event Grid custom topic to obtain its endpoint and access key
Create an event subscription on the topic with a filter and the webhook endpoint as the destination
Publish events to the topic endpoint, authenticating with the access key
The handler receives only the events that satisfy the subscription's filter

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B, C, D):** First create the custom topic for its endpoint and key, then add a subscription defining the filter and webhook destination, then publish events to the endpoint using the key, after which only matching events reach the handler. Why the others are wrong: **B** can't precede **A** since a subscription needs an existing topic; **C** before **B** publishes events with nothing to route them; **D** is the end result, not a setup step.
